passage: My name is Arnab. In Class Six some boys call me "Tummy Bear." At first I laughed, because everyone laughed and I didn't want to be the one who couldn't take a joke. So I laughed every day, even when my ears went hot. On Tuesday I walked home slowly, feeling as if the laugh had been stuck to my face. Disha, who sits beside me, caught up and said, "You didn't look like you were enjoying that." I shrugged. She said, "You can tell Ma'am, you know. It's not being sensitive." I still don't know how I feel. That night I told my mother, and she held my hand and said we'd speak to the teacher together.

qa.q: What do some boys call Arnab in Class Six?
qa.a: "Tummy Bear."

qa.q: What was Arnab feeling while laughing along, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Ashamed and hurt. Arnab's ears went hot and the laugh felt stuck to the face, even though Arnab did not want to seem unable to take a joke.

qa.q: What choice helped Arnab after Disha spoke?
qa.a: Arnab told the mother that night, and she listened and offered to speak to the teacher together.

qa.q: How does Disha see the situation?
qa.a: Disha noticed that Arnab was not enjoying the joke and said that telling Ma'am is not being sensitive, which shows Disha sees the hurt behind the laugh.

grounding: A child laughs along at nicknames about their body while feeling ashamed, and Disha notices the hurt.

passage:
Note from Madhav, class teacher, Thursday.
During the break I saw Kunal call Kishore "Football" again, and the others laughed. Kishore laughed too, but it stopped at the mouth; the eyes were on the floor, and the hands kept pulling at the shirt. Not wanting to make it worse in front of the class, I waited until the corridor was empty and said, "That looked like it hurt, and it's not your fault." Kishore looked away and said, "It's just a joke." I said I would still speak to the school counsellor that day. I did, and I spoke to Kunal separately. I will check in with Kishore again tomorrow morning.

qa.q: What did Kunal call Kishore during the break?
qa.a: "Football."

qa.q: What does Kishore's laugh that stopped at the mouth suggest about how Kishore feels?
qa.a: Hurt or ashamed underneath. The eyes stayed on the floor and the hands pulled at the shirt, though Kishore said it was just a joke.

qa.q: What did Madhav do the same day?
qa.a: Madhav spoke to Kishore privately, said it was not Kishore's fault, told the school counsellor and spoke to Kunal separately.

qa.q: How might Kishore feel when Madhav says "That looked like it hurt, and it's not your fault"?
qa.a: Possibly relieved to be noticed, though still guarded, since Kishore looked away and repeated "It's just a joke."

grounding: A child laughs along at nicknames about their body while hurting inside, and an adult notices and acts the same day.

passage:
"How was school, Reena?"
"Fine." Reena dropped her bag. Karthik, her big brother, looked up from his homework.
"You're not fine. What happened?"
"Nothing. They call me 'Stick' because my legs are thin. It's funny."
"Is it?"
Reena shrugged. "I laugh. If I don't, they'll say I can't take a joke."
"But how does it feel?"
Reena's chin wobbled. "Bad. Like my legs are wrong."
Karthik put his pen down. "Your legs are fine. And it's not your fault. I'm telling Mummy, okay?"
He called Mummy in from the kitchen. She sat on the bed and listened to all of it. "Thank you for telling us, Reena. This isn't okay, and it's not because you're too sensitive. I'll call your class teacher tonight."

qa.q: What do the other children call Reena?
qa.a: Stick.

qa.q: What was Reena feeling while laughing along?
qa.a: She felt ashamed and hurt, as if her legs were wrong, but was afraid of being called too sensitive.

qa.q: What did Karthik and Mummy do that same day?
qa.a: Karthik listened and told Mummy at once; Mummy listened, said it wasn't Reena's fault, and planned to call the class teacher that night.

qa.q: How might Karthik have felt when Reena admitted it felt bad?
qa.a: He was probably protective and concerned, putting down his pen and acting right away.

grounding: Shows a child laughing along at a body nickname while feeling ashamed, and adults responding the same day when she tells.

passage:
In Class 6, Tarun started calling me "Balloon" because I was the roundest boy in the class. The whole row laughed, and so did I. I even puffed my cheeks out once, to be funny.
But every night, I pulled my shirt down over my stomach in the mirror. I stopped eating my tiffin at school. I didn't want anyone to see me eat.
I didn't say anything, because I didn't want to be the one who can't take a joke.
One day, the PE sir saw me sitting alone at lunch with my full tiffin. He sat down and asked, "Thomas, is something wrong?" I told him everything. He said, "Laughing along doesn't mean it didn't hurt. Thank you for telling me." That afternoon he spoke to Tarun and called my mother.
Tarun hasn't said it since.

qa.q: What did Tarun call Thomas?
qa.a: Balloon.

qa.q: What was Thomas feeling while laughing along?
qa.a: Thomas felt ashamed and hurt, hiding his stomach in the mirror and not eating at school.

qa.q: What did the PE sir do that helped?
qa.a: He noticed Thomas alone, listened, said laughing along didn't mean it didn't hurt, and that same afternoon spoke to Tarun and called his mother.

qa.q: How might Tarun have seen the nickname at first?
qa.a: Tarun probably thought it was just a funny joke, since Thomas laughed and even puffed his cheeks.

grounding: Shows a child laughing along at a body nickname while feeling ashamed, afraid of seeming too sensitive, and an adult responding the same day.

passage:
Class 5 teacher's note, Tuesday.
During group work, I heard some children call Ritu (10) "Giraffe" because she is the tallest in the class. Ritu laughed and bent her knees to look shorter. But I noticed she hunched in her seat for the rest of the day, and at break she stood alone. Her friend Uma told me quietly that Ritu had been crying in the washroom.
I spoke to Ritu after the bell. She said, "It's just a joke, ma'am. I don't want them to think I'm a baby." I told her that laughing along doesn't mean it doesn't hurt, and that she was right to feel upset. I thanked Uma for telling me.
I spoke to the group before home time, called Ritu's mother this evening, and will check in with Ritu tomorrow.

qa.q: What did the children call Ritu?
qa.a: Giraffe.

qa.q: What was Ritu feeling when she laughed and bent her knees?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and ashamed of her height, laughing along so she wouldn't seem like a baby.

qa.q: What did the teacher do the same day?
qa.a: The teacher spoke to Ritu, told her it was okay to feel hurt, thanked Uma, spoke to the group before home time and called Ritu's mother that evening.

qa.q: How might Uma have felt telling the teacher?
qa.a: Uma was probably worried for Ritu and relieved to tell an adult who would help.

grounding: Shows a child laughing along at a nickname about her body while ashamed inside, and a teacher responding the same day.

passage:
Tuesday
Kamal's diary. Pradeep called me "Motu Kamal" again at PT. Then "Laddoo". Everyone laughed, so I laughed too, louder than them, and patted my stomach like it was funny. It's not funny. My ears were hot for the whole period. I didn't say stop, because then they'll say I can't take a joke and I'm too sensitive, and that's worse.
At dinner I didn't want roti. Mamma asked why. I didn't plan to tell her but it came out. She put down her plate and just listened. She said laughing along doesn't mean it doesn't hurt, and it isn't being too sensitive. She wrote to Ms Fernandes on the school message app right then, and showed me what she wrote.

qa.q: What names did Pradeep call Kamal at PT?
qa.a: He called Kamal "Motu Kamal" and "Laddoo".

qa.q: Why did Kamal laugh louder than everyone else?
qa.a: Kamal felt ashamed and hurt but was afraid of being called too sensitive, so laughing along felt safer.

qa.q: What did Mamma do that helped?
qa.a: She stopped eating to listen, told Kamal it isn't being too sensitive, and wrote to Ms Fernandes that same evening, showing Kamal the message.

qa.q: How might Pradeep see Kamal's laughing along?
qa.a: He may think Kamal enjoys the nicknames, because the loud laugh hides how hurt Kamal is.

grounding: Shows a child laughing along at body-based nicknames while feeling ashamed, and a parent taking the hurt seriously the same day.
